## 1. Identification Strategy  
Instrumental‐Variables (2SLS) design.  
We exploit cohort-by-state variation in compulsory–schooling and child-labor laws (CSLs) in place when individuals were 14.  These laws shifted schooling upward differentially across state-cohorts but were written 30 years before wages are observed, long before the later labor-market shocks that might contaminate wages.  By using the CSLs as instruments for (i) an individual’s own years of schooling and (ii) the average schooling of other workers in the same state-by-census year, we can separate private from “external” returns.  The first stage is strong (high-school movement produced 0.3–1.0 additional grades), and the exclusion restriction is plausible because CSLs should affect adult wages only through education decisions.

## 2. Treatment and Control  

Treatment variable (endogenous regressor of interest)  
• 𝑆̄ _st: Average completed grades among 16-64 year-olds in state s, census year t, computed with survey weights and excluding the individual i (“leave-one-out”).  

Secondary endogenous regressor  
• S_i: individual i’s own completed grades.  

Instrument set  
• CSL_index_sb: a vector summarising the five CSL dimensions in the state of birth s when cohort b (i’s birth year) turned 14.  
• (Optionally) the same variables defined for the state of residence to instrument S̄ if in-migration is substantial.

Treated vs. control cohorts  
• “Treated” = state-cohorts facing stricter CSLs (higher minimum dropout age, etc.).  
• “Control” = state-cohorts facing laxer CSLs or no change.  

Timing  
• Event year = calendar year individual’s cohort turned 14.  After that point laws are fixed for that cohort.  

No running variable / cutoff – not an RDD.

## 3. Key Identifying Assumptions  

A1 (Relevance). CSLs must predict both individual and average schooling.  
Plausible: historic evidence shows large enrollment responses to law changes.

A2 (Exclusion). Conditional on fixed effects and controls, CSLs affect adult wages only through schooling (own or peers), not through other channels such as contemporaneous economic development.  
Plausible because CSLs were enacted mainly for educational/child-welfare reasons decades earlier.  We further absorb state-of-birth and cohort fixed effects and state-specific linear trends.

A3 (Independence). There were no simultaneous state-cohort shocks (e.g., manufacturing booms) that both encouraged CSL passage and permanently raised wages.  
More plausible once we control for pre-existing state income, urbanisation, and region × cohort effects.

A4 (SUTVA / stable composition). One individual’s treatment status (education) affects another’s outcome only through the measured peer-schooling variable and within-state labour markets. Cross-state spillovers are small.  
Reasonable given frictions in inter-state commuting for the 1950–90 period, but we will test robustness by excluding border states.

A5 (Monotonicity). Stricter CSLs weakly increase schooling for everyone (no group systematically decreases schooling when laws tighten).  
Supported by prior micro evidence on CSLs.

## 4. Main Threats and Mitigating Actions  

T1. Policy endogeneity: Progressive, high-growth states may both pass stricter CSLs and experience faster long-run wage growth.  
• Include state-of-birth fixed effects, cohort fixed effects, and state-specific linear (or quadratic) birth-year trends.  
• Add controls for pre-law state characteristics (manufacturing share, urbanisation in 1910) interacted with cohort trends (“flexible controls”).  
• Placebo check: run the same IV on pre-treatment cohorts (born before 1885) to confirm zero “effect”.

T2. Selective migration dilutes or biases the peer-schooling measure.  
• Baseline sample restricted to men living in their birth state at census date.  
• Show robustness including migrants, instrumenting with CSLs in state of birth but measuring peer schooling in state of residence; adjust SEs for two-way clustering.  
• Estimate migration propensity as a function of CSLs to show no systematic sorting.

T3. Common-shock bias within states (e.g., defence procurement in WWII).  
• Control for census-year × region fixed effects; alternatively, interact national sectoral shocks with initial state industry mix (Bartik controls).  
• Cluster standard errors at the state-of-birth level to acknowledge serial correlation.

## 5. R Code Outline  

```r
# ---- 0. Packages ----
library(data.table)
library(fixest)   # fast OLS / IV with high-dimensional FE
library(sandwich)
library(modelsummary)

# ---- 1. Load micro data ----
# Assume three CSVs:
#  ipums.csv  (one row per individual)
#  csl.csv    (state-by-year compulsory schooling law variables, 1914-1965)
#  state_cov.csv (baseline 1910 covariates by state)

ipums <- fread("ipums.csv")  # 1950-1990 pooled
csl   <- fread("csl.csv")
covs  <- fread("state_cov.csv")

# ---- 2. Variable construction ----
# Keep baseline sample: U.S.-born white men age 40-49
ipums <- ipums[age >= 40 & age <= 49 & race == "white" & sex == "male" & born_US == 1]

# Individual schooling (truncate at 17)
ipums[, S_i := pmin(educ, 17)]

# Log weekly wage
ipums[, lww := log(wage_annual / weeks_worked)]

# Birth cohort (year of birth)
ipums[, cohort := birth_year]

# Merge CSLs – laws in state of birth when cohort age = 14
csl[, law_year := year]                       # explicit
ipums[, age14_year := cohort + 14]
setkey(csl, state, law_year)
ipums <- csl[ipums, roll = TRUE, on = .(state = state_birth,
                                        law_year = age14_year)]

# Construct CSL index (e.g., first PC or sum of standardised components)
csls <- c("max_enroll_age", "min_dropout_age",
          "req_school_years", "min_work_age", "school_for_work_permit")
for(v in csls) csl[, (v) := scale(get(v))]
csl[, CSL_index := rowMeans(.SD, na.rm=TRUE), .SDcols = csls]

ipums <- merge(ipums, csl[, .(state_birth = state,
                               cohort = birth_year,
                               CSL_index)], by = c("state_birth","cohort"))

# ---- 3. Peer (state-year) average schooling ----
# Compute leave-one-out mean schooling
ipums[, weight := popwt]   # person weight * weeks worked if provided
peer <- ipums[, .(S_bar = weighted.mean(S_i, w = weight)),
              by = .(state_res, census_year)]
ipums <- merge(ipums, peer, by = c("state_res","census_year"))

# ---- 4. Main IV regression ----
# Formula: log wage on own schooling + peer schooling, instrumented with CSL index
fe_formula <- lww ~ S_i + S_bar | 0 |
  S_i + S_bar ~ CSL_index + I(CSL_index * 0) # same instrument for both

# Using fixest syntax: dep_var ~ endog | fixed | instruments
iv_main <- feols(lww ~ 1 | state_birth + cohort + census_year ~
                 S_i + S_bar | CSL_index + CSL_index,
                 data = ipums, cluster = ~state_birth)

summary(iv_main)

# ---- 5. Robustness: restrict to non-migrants ----
iv_nomig <- feols(lww ~ 1 | state_birth + cohort + census_year ~
                  S_i + S_bar | CSL_index + CSL_index,
                  data = ipums[state_birth == state_res],
                  cluster = ~state_birth)

# Present results
modelsummary(list(Main = iv_main, NonMigrants = iv_nomig),
             estimate = "{estimate} ({std.error})",
             statistic = NULL,
             stars = TRUE)
```

Key notes:  
• fixest places high-dimensional fixed effects quickly.  
• We cluster by state of birth to respect the level at which the instrument varies.  
• The same CSL_index is used as an instrument for both S_i and S̄; identification comes from differential impacts on own vs. peer schooling after controlling for the other.

## 6. Expected Results  

Economic theory predicts positive externalities: a more educated workforce improves knowledge spillovers, productivity, and complements physical capital.  Prior U.S. cross-state regressions suggest private returns ≈ 7–9 percent per year of schooling.  I expect an external return of roughly 1–3 percent per additional mean grade in the state.  Hence a one-grade increase in average schooling would raise individual wages by ≈ 2 percent holding own education constant – non-trivial but an order of magnitude smaller than private returns and not large enough on its own to explain the full cross-state or cross-country income gap.

## 7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (IV)  

C1 Relevance of instrument (F-stat > 10)  … 1  
C2 Exclusion from adult wages except via schooling … 0.7  
C3 Independence from state-specific wage shocks … 0.7  
C4 Monotonicity / no defiers … 1  
C5 SUTVA / limited spillovers across states … 0.6  

Total ≈ 4/5.  Items 2, 3, 5 remain potential concerns but are addressed through fixed effects, robustness checks, and sample restrictions.
